content.text: A well half remembered is worse than a well forgotten outright, because it invites you to gamble on it. Memory keeps the details it wants and discards the ones it decides, later, were never essential. A well-kept ledger tells you less about money than it does about the person who kept it.

We crossed the flats at night to spare the animals, and the stars there were more numerous than I had words for. The city at that hour belonged mostly to delivery carts and the occasional insomniac. Old letters, reread, always sound slightly more confident than the person who wrote them actually was.

The merchant's ledger recorded debts in three languages and grudges, I suspect, in a fourth known only to him. A door left ajar in an old house creaks in a key entirely its own. The harvest that year came in later than usual, and no less welcome for it.

Salt traders measure distance in wells, not miles, which tells you plainly what the desert considers important. Silence between two people who know each other well is rarely uncomfortable. The workshop light stayed on past midnight more nights than either of us cared to count.

A rumour from the last oasis reached us garbled, as rumours do, but garbled in a direction that turned out to be true. A path worn into a lawn tells you exactly where people actually wanted the path to be. The sea keeps no calendar, which is either its great honesty or its great indifference.

The caravan camped a half day short of the crossing rather than risk the flats in failing light. An old friend visiting after years away brings the past with them, uninvited but not unwelcome. The bread was better that winter, though no one could say exactly why.

I have crossed the salt road twice now, and both times arrived a slightly different person than the one who set out. A long apprenticeship teaches humility faster than it teaches skill, and in the correct order. The train timetable was more aspiration than fact, and everyone along the line understood as much.

A guide's reputation rests entirely on wells that are there when he says they will be, and nothing else. A candle burns down evenly only if you trim the wick, a lesson repeated in every household. The orchard gave less fruit that year but of a better, denser sweetness.

The flats at midday are silent in a way that presses on the ears, absence made almost audible. A stranger's kindness on a hard day is remembered longer than most kindnesses from family. The wind off the water carried salt far enough inland to whiten the window glass by spring.

We traded cloth for water at the last oasis, a rate the merchant called fair and I called fortunate. A journal kept honestly becomes, without meaning to, a kind of second memory. The market emptied by four, leaving only the smell of what had been sold there.

The salt road does not forgive confidence, only preparation, and even then only some of the time. An old dog knows the sound of the right footsteps long before anyone else in the house does. The harvest moon that year hung low enough to seem, briefly, close.

The salt flats took the light and threw it back doubled, until the horizon stopped meaning anything in particular. A debt repaid on time is remembered less than one repaid a day late. The workshop smelled of sawdust and, faintly, of the coffee no one ever finished.

A caravan at dusk moves slower than it does at noon, as though the animals too feel the day loosening its grip. A letter that arrives too late still says something true, even if the moment has passed. The garden wall held the day's heat long after the sun itself had gone down.

The well at the crossing was half remembered by every guide who claimed to know it, which worried me more than an honest no. An empty house is loud in a way a full one never manages to be. The apprentice years pass slowly at the time and quickly in the remembering.

Merchants kept their ledgers in a shorthand no customs officer ever fully cracked, and none of them explained why. A well-worn tool fits the hand better than any new one, however well made. The evening train was always half empty, and always exactly on time.

Rumour travelled faster across the flats than any caravan, arriving at the last oasis a full day ahead of us. An old photograph tells you what a person looked like and almost nothing about who they were. The bakery opened before the rest of the street had decided the day had begun.

The salt crust cracked under the camels' feet in a sound like distant, patient applause. A long correspondence, kept up faithfully, is its own kind of small monument. The frost came early that year and stripped the orchard almost overnight.

A trader I met twice, years apart, told the same story both times with a different ending, and I preferred the second. An honest account of a hard season reads, afterward, like a much easier one than it was. The workshop door stuck in wet weather, a fault no one ever quite got around to fixing.

At the last oasis the water tasted faintly of salt regardless, a joke the desert never tired of telling. A river town keeps different hours than a market town, and neither much minds the other's. The last light of the day fell across the table in a way that made finishing supper feel unhurried.

The caravan master read the sky the way other men read a ledger, and trusted it about as much. An old coat, kept for sentiment, still fits better than most people expect. The harbor quieted by evening to the sound of ropes against the pilings and little else.

A neighbor's lamp, lit before dawn, was as good as a clock to anyone passing. The season turned the way seasons do, without asking anyone's permission first. An unfinished letter is, in its way, more honest than a finished one.

The workshop ledger recorded debts in pencil and settlements in ink, and rarely confused the two. A well-worn path through a wood is a kind of quiet agreement among everyone who uses it. The morning fog burned off by nine most days, later on the days it mattered least.

An old friend's handwriting is recognisable at a glance, long after the face has grown less familiar. The market square filled slowly and emptied all at once, as though on a signal no one gave aloud. A garden gate left open is, more often than not, simply an invitation no one has withdrawn.

The lamp oil was rationed that winter, and the evenings grew, by necessity, quieter for it. An old ledger, found later, tells a fuller story than the person who kept it ever meant to leave behind. The wind changed direction twice in a single afternoon, which the fishermen took as its own kind of warning.

A long winter makes the first warm day feel larger than the weather alone accounts for. The workshop's apprentices came and went, but the smell of the place never really changed. An orchard in bloom is briefly, almost embarrassingly, more beautiful than it has any right to be.

The evening post brought less news than expected and somehow felt heavier for it. A house passed down through a family keeps, in its floors and doorframes, a record no deed can match. The harbor at first light belonged to the gulls and the earliest of the fishing boats.
